title: Implement Insertion Sort — pick each element and insert it in its correct position in the already sorted part; O(n²) but fast for nearly sorted data.

s1_definition.profdef: Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by taking the next unsorted element, called the key, and inserting it into its correct position within the already sorted prefix, shifting larger elements one step to the right to make room. It has quadratic time in the worst case but linear time on nearly sorted data, uses constant extra space, and is stable. It is efficient for small or almost-sorted inputs and is the algorithm used inside hybrid sorts for small subarrays.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India sorting a hand of balance cards the way you sort playing cards. She holds a sorted group in her left hand and picks up the next card with her right. She slides that card leftward past every card bigger than it until it sits in the right spot, then picks up the next one. The left hand is always sorted; each new card is simply inserted where it belongs.
s1_definition.oneliner: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by inserting each new element into its correct place, shifting bigger ones aside.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by taking the next unsorted element, called the key, and inserting it into its correct position within the already sorted prefix, shifting larger elements one step to the right to make room. It has quadratic time in the worst case but linear time on nearly sorted data, uses constant extra space, and is stable. It is efficient for small or almost-sorted inputs and is the algorithm used inside hybrid sorts for small subarrays.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India sorting a hand of balance cards the way you sort playing cards. She holds a sorted group in her left hand and picks up the next card with her right. She slides that card leftward past every card bigger than it until it sits in the right spot, then picks up the next one. The left hand is always sorted; each new card is simply inserted where it belongs.

**One line to remember:** Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by inserting each new element into its correct place, shifting bigger ones aside.

sections.s2_technical:
Insertion sort treats the first element as a trivially sorted prefix of length one, then extends the prefix one element at a time. For each new key it walks backward through the sorted prefix, shifting every element larger than the key one position to the right, and then drops the key into the gap.

The inner loop does the shifting. We save the key with `BigDecimal key = arr[i];`, then `int j = i - 1; while (j >= 0 && arr[j].compareTo(key) > 0) { arr[j + 1] = arr[j]; j--; }` slides larger elements right, and finally `arr[j + 1] = key;` places the key. Notice the condition uses strictly greater than, which is what makes insertion sort stable: equal elements are not shifted past each other, so their original order is preserved.

The reason it excels on nearly sorted data is that if an element is already in place, the inner while loop does zero shifts and exits immediately. On fully sorted input every key stops instantly, giving linear time. This adaptivity is its signature strength and the reason it is chosen for the small-subarray base case inside TimSort and introsort.

A senior-level point is that insertion sort is the practical winner among the simple sorts for small arrays, often faster than the fancy n log n sorts below a threshold of around ten to twenty elements because it has tiny constant factors and no recursion overhead. That is exactly why production library sorts switch to insertion sort for small pieces. It is stable and in place. Its weakness is quadratic behaviour on large, randomly ordered data, where the backward shifts dominate, so it is not a general-purpose large-scale sort.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India maintains a running sorted list of the day's transaction amounts, and new transactions trickle in one at a time throughout the day. Each new amount must slot into the already sorted list in the correct place. Inserting one element at a time into a sorted sequence is precisely what insertion sort does.

Problem 2 — Because the list is kept sorted continuously, each new arrival is usually close to its final position, so the data is nearly sorted. Insertion sort runs in nearly linear time on such data because most insertions require very few shifts, which makes it the ideal fit for this incremental, almost-sorted workload.

In our mini-project we build an `InsertionSorter` that sorts an array of BigDecimal amounts ascending, logging how the sorted prefix grows and how many shifts each insertion needs. The demo sorts a small, nearly sorted array of the bank's amounts and shows the efficient shifting.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the array 1000, 3000, 7500, 3500, 9000, which is nearly sorted.

Step 1: The prefix starts as just 1000. We take the key 3000 at index one. We compare it with 1000; 1000 is not larger, so zero shifts, and 3000 stays in place. The prefix is 1000, 3000.

Step 2: We take the key 7500. Compare with 3000; not larger, zero shifts. 7500 stays. The prefix is 1000, 3000, 7500.

Step 3: We take the key 3500. Compare with 7500; 7500 is larger, so shift it right. Compare with 3000; not larger, stop. One shift. We drop 3500 into the gap, giving 1000, 3000, 3500, 7500.

Step 4: We take the key 9000. Compare with 7500; not larger, zero shifts. 9000 stays at the end.

Step 5: The array is now fully sorted. Notice the total shifts across the whole run were just one, because the data was nearly sorted. This is why insertion sort is so fast on such input.

Step 6: The final array is 1000, 3000, 3500, 7500, 9000, sorted ascending in place, with equal elements, had there been any, keeping their original order.

```

[2026-10-26 20:50:02] INFO    Insert 3000 at position 1 after 0 shift(s) → [1000, 3000, 7500, 3500, 9000]
[2026-10-26 20:50:02] INFO    Insert 7500 at position 2 after 0 shift(s) → [1000, 3000, 7500, 3500, 9000]
[2026-10-26 20:50:02] INFO    Insert 3500 at position 2 after 1 shift(s) → [1000, 3000, 3500, 7500, 9000]
[2026-10-26 20:50:02] INFO    Insert 9000 at position 4 after 0 shift(s) → [1000, 3000, 3500, 7500, 9000]
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Insertion Sort ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Incremental build: extend sorted prefix one key at a time     │
  │  Shift-then-insert: strict '>' keeps it stable and adaptive    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: InsertionSorter only sorts                               │
  │  O: used as the small-array base case inside hybrid sorts     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            InsertionSorter            │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + sortAscending(arr): void           │  O(n²) worst, O(n) nearly sorted
  │                                        │  O(1) space, STABLE
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      invariant: arr[0..i-1] sorted; key inserted into it

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. for i=1..n-1: key=arr[i]
  2. shift arr[j] right while arr[j] > key
  3. arr[j+1] = key
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time. It treats the first element as a sorted prefix of length one, then takes each next element as a key and inserts it into its correct place within the sorted prefix, shifting every larger element one step to the right to open a gap. It has quadratic time in the worst case, uses only constant extra memory, and is stable.

Its signature strength, which I always emphasise, is adaptivity. If an element is already in place, the inner shifting loop does nothing and exits immediately, so on fully sorted or nearly sorted data insertion sort runs in nearly linear time. I also point out that using a strict greater-than comparison when shifting is what keeps it stable, because equal elements are never shifted past one another.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this idea for a running sorted list of the day's transaction amounts. New transactions arrive one at a time, and each must slot into the already sorted list in the right position, which is exactly insertion. Because the list stays sorted continuously, each new arrival is close to its final spot, so insertions need very few shifts and the whole thing stays fast.

The senior-level point I make is that insertion sort is the practical winner among the simple sorts for small arrays. Below a threshold of roughly ten to twenty elements it often beats the fancier n log n sorts because it has tiny constant factors and no recursion overhead, which is precisely why production library sorts like TimSort switch to insertion sort for small subarrays. Its weakness is large, randomly ordered data, where the backward shifts dominate and it degrades to quadratic time. So I use it for small or nearly sorted inputs and as a building block, and I rely on the full library sort for large general data.
